after.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula 

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, ${f}_{1}(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the upper semicircle and ${f}_{2}(x)=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the lower semicircle with $a=0$ and $b=6.$ 

First, we find the derivative of ${f}_{1}(x):$

$$
{f}_{1}^{′}(x)=\frac{3-x}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Substituting ${f}_{1}^{′}(x)$ into the arc length formula, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{1} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}_{1}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+\frac{(3-x)^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{\frac{6x-{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}+\frac{9-6x+{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In the same manner, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L={L}_{1}+{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{6}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula 

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, ${f}_{1}(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the upper semicircle and ${f}_{2}(x)=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the lower semicircle with $a=0$ and $b=6.$ 

First, we find the derivative of ${f}_{1}(x):$

$$
{f}_{1}^{′}(x)=\frac{3-x}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Substituting ${f}_{1}^{′}(x)$ into the arc length formula, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{1} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}_{1}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+\frac{(3-x)^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{\frac{6x-{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}+\frac{9-6x+{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In the same manner, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L={L}_{1}+{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{6}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider a circle with radius $3$ centered at the point $(3,0),$ shown above.

Earlier part 1:

Earlier part 2:

Earlier part 3:

Current part:

Construct an integral that represents the arc length of this circle in rectangular coordinates.

content.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula 

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, ${f}_{1}(x)=\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the upper semicircle and ${f}_{2}(x)=-\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}$ represents the lower semicircle with $a=0$ and $b=6.$ 

First, we find the derivative of ${f}_{1}(x):$

$$
{f}_{1}^{′}(x)=\frac{3-x}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Substituting ${f}_{1}^{′}(x)$ into the arc length formula, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{1} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}_{1}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{1+\frac{(3-x)^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\sqrt{\frac{6x-{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}+\frac{9-6x+{x}^{2}}{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In the same manner, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L={L}_{1}+{L}_{2} & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{3}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{6}{\sqrt{6x-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ and the rays $\theta ={\theta }_{1}$ and $\theta ={\theta }_{2}$ is given by the formula

$$

$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{[\frac{\pi }{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})]}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }(6-(-6)) \\  & =\frac{12}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$
